content: SIM2, or Single-minded homolog 2, is a protein encoded by the SIM2 gene in humans. This protein plays a critical role in the development of the central nervous system's midline, as well as in the formation of facial and cranial structures. The SIM2 gene is a homolog of the Drosophila single-minded (sim) gene, which encodes a transcription factor that serves as a master regulator of neurogenesis in midline cells of the central nervous system. The SIM2 gene is located on the q arm of chromosome 21, specifically at band 22.2, within the Down syndrome chromosomal region. Due to its location, its function as a transcriptional repressor, and its similarity to the Drosophila sim gene, it is hypothesized that SIM2 may contribute to certain phenotypes associated with Down syndrome. SIM2 interacts with the Aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator. When the SIM2 gene is introduced into PC12 cells, it disrupts the normal cell maturation cycle. SIM2 inhibits the expression of cyclin E, which prevents cells from progressing through the G1/S checkpoint of the cell cycle, thereby suppressing cell proliferation. Additionally, SIM2 upregulates the expression of p27, a protein that inhibits growth. The presence of p27 further suppresses the activation of cell cycle regulatory kinases. The SIM2 gene can exist in three states: +/+, +/-, and -/-. When the gene is in the SIM2 -/state, it is considered disrupted, leading to significant physical malformations, particularly in the craniofacial region. Individuals with the SIM2 -/state often exhibit a full or partial cleft of the secondary palate, as well as malformations of the tongue and the pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone. These abnormalities result in aerophagia, or the swallowing of air, which can lead to postnatal death. Severe aerophagia causes air to accumulate in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to abdominal distension. Overexpression of the SIM2 gene is thought to contribute to some of the phenotypic abnormalities observed in Down syndrome. SIM2 mRNA has been detected in various regions of the brain that are known to exhibit deformities in individuals with Down syndrome, as well as in the palate, oral and tongue epithelia, and the mandibular and hyoid bones. There are two known isoforms of SIM2, each with distinct roles in different tissues. One of these isoforms, SIM2 Short (SIM2s), is specifically expressed in mammary gland tissue. SIM2s is a splice variant of SIM2 that lacks exon 11. Research has shown that SIM2s plays a role in mammary gland development and exhibits tumor-suppressive properties, particularly in breast cancer. In mouse models, the absence of SIM2s expression in mammary epithelial cells leads to developmental defects resembling cancerous characteristics. These defects include increased cell proliferation, invasion of local stroma, loss of cellular polarity, and reduced expression of E-cadherin, a molecule critical for cell adhesion. These findings suggest that SIM2s is essential for normal mammary gland development. Experiments reintroducing SIM2s into human breast cancer cells have demonstrated its tumor-suppressive effects. Immunohistochemical staining has shown that SIM2s is more highly expressed in normal human breast cells compared to cancerous ones. Reintroducing SIM2s into breast cancer cells results in reduced growth, proliferation, and invasiveness. SIM2s suppresses the activity of the matrix metalloprotease-3 (MMP3) gene, which is involved in cell migration, cancer progression, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions (EMT). SIM2s also represses the SLUG transcription factor, which further inhibits EMT. By suppressing EMT, SIM2s preserves E-cadherin expression and prevents pathological EMT associated with tumor formation. These findings highlight the tumor-suppressive role of SIM2s in mammary epithelial cells. To study the effects of SIM2 disruption, scientists can create a knockout model of the gene. This is achieved through homologous recombination, which eliminates the predicted start codon and the subsequent 47 amino acids of the gene. An EcoRI restriction site is then introduced into the chromosome to facilitate further analysis.
